_comment: Chapter 1 cue sheet. All 20 assets are approved and generated.
A cue says WHEN an asset plays. It never defines the asset; that lives in
audio/sfx-registry.json and is shared with later chapters and with Godot.
ANCHORS, NOT TIMESTAMPS. Each cue points at a voice segment by its clipId plus
WHICH occurrence of that clip it is. The occurrence matters: a clipId can appear
twice in one chapter, and five do here -- "Yep.", "I know.", "Jack.", "Jack
nodded." and "Request denied." are each one asset heard twice. Regenerating a
voice clip changes its length but not its identity, and inserting a paragraph
shifts every absolute time but no anchor, which is why timestamps are computed
for human review only and are never the synchronisation mechanism.
timing: `before` plays the cue in the gap ahead of that segment, `after` in the
gap behind it, `during` starts it offsetMs into the segment. A sustained cue
starts at its anchor and stops at sustain.until.
gain here overrides the category default in audio/config.json. Every number is a
starting point for Joshua's ear, not a finished mix.
35 events, 20 unique assets after Joshua's first listen. The six typing cues added
then are all the SAME keyboard asset the chapter already used, so more typing cost
nothing: it is one generated sound heard nine times. Long stretches are still
deliberately voices and room tone and nothing else.
2026-09-18: the keyboard cues' gains are PROVISIONAL and currently have no audible
effect. Measurement showed the keyboard asset is -46.9 dBFS RMS with a 3-second file
that sounds for 0.00s -- a few faint ticks in near-silence -- so no gain makes typing
audible under speech at about -22 dB. They are set to 0.42-0.55, which is right for a
correctly levelled asset, rather than left at the 0.85 I had tried: 0.85 of a good
recording would be far too loud. Re-measure once the asset is replaced.

cues.why: Enters on 'Deep inside one of those laboratories' -- the sentence that puts us in the room -- and never leaves, because the chapter never leaves. Establishes an occupied but near-empty building at night so that every later silence reads as a room and not as dead air. GAIN 0.08 -> 0.2: Joshua could not hear the room tone at all. 0.08 against a voice reference of 1.0 is roughly -22 dB, which is below the floor of a phone speaker in a room.

The listener hears the chirp, then the narrator says a warning tone chirped. Putting it first makes the sound the event and the narration the confirmation, which is how the scene actually happens to Jack.
The same asset, louder, because the manuscript says the second tone was louder than the first. One generated sound covers both, and the escalation is done with gain rather than with a second file.

The alarm does not stop when the sentence does -- the manuscript has the warning repeating and a second alarm sounding later. A low looping bed under the opening carries that, ducks hard beneath speech, and fades out after 'That's impossible', which is where the scene stops shouting and starts being strange. GAIN 0.2 -> 0.15: Joshua's instruction: turn the alarm bed down. EMPHASIS DROPPED TO 0 on 2026-09-19. The +6.0/+8.3 here were raising the one sound Joshua said he could not hear the narrator past, and they were chosen when the mix was placed by RMS -- which reads this asset 3 to 6 dB quieter than the ear does. With loudness measured properly the category target is already where this moment should sit.
Gives the alarm a physical consequence in a body rather than only on a screen. It is the one sound in the chapter that tells the listener how hard Jack was asleep.
Lands on 'Jack grabbed the keyboard'. Establishes that he is working the problem with his hands, which is what makes the later moment when the cursor moves by itself frightening.
Jack entering a command and running a second search. The manuscript has him working the logs by hand here, and it was silent.
One sharp hit on 'Another alarm sounded'. Distinct from the opening eruption: this is the system finding something new, not the system panicking.
The manuscript says the system beeped and a directory opened by itself. A calm, polite notification is more unsettling here than an alarm would be -- the machine is not warning him, it is working.
It has to sound like the lock worked, or the terminal coming back on by itself is not a violation.
Three seconds of black screen and then the machine wakes itself. Placed after the narration so the listener hears the thing happen having just been told it would not.
Jack's 'Sarah?' has to arrive into an open channel, or the listener does not know he is talking to a wall. This is the cue that changes the acoustic space for the next twenty segments.

A faint live-channel hiss under the whole intercom exchange is the only way to make Sarah read as remote without filtering her approved voice clips. One asset covers twenty segments and nothing of hers is regenerated. GAIN 0.06 -> 0.14: Quieter than the bed he could not hear, so it cannot have been audible either -- and an inaudible intercom bed cannot be judged, which is what he approved it to test.
The manuscript makes static the answer to his question. It is the scene's reply, so it plays before the line that names it.
'Jack tapped the button again' -- the same asset, slightly quieter. The repeat is the information: he is not getting an answer.
Closes the frame cue ch01-070 opened. Without it the listener has no signal that Sarah's channel is gone, and the room he is left alone in is the point of the next four segments.

'Jack froze as a file opened', then TOMBS says Boundary control. Reusing the same calm notification ties this to the directory opening earlier: it is the same intruder, doing the same unhurried thing.
The manuscript puts the door mid-sentence and behind him. The listener should know someone is in the room a beat before Jack does.
Someone entering is one of the few things footsteps are for. Soft rubber soles on a hard floor, because Chapter 1 canon puts her in gray sneakers.
'as she walked over' -- the second and last time the chapter hears her walk. It moves her from the doorway to Jack's shoulder, which is where she stays.
Two people arranging themselves around one workstation. The chairs are how the chapter shows them working as a pair, and it is worth hearing once.
The same asset closing the small joke that started with 'Move.' Jack gives up the keyboard, physically.
'Sarah immediately started typing' -- the moment the competent one takes over. Marking who has the keyboard is the scene's quiet shift of authority.
Sarah opening the connection history. She has the keyboard now and the scene should keep saying so.
“began digging through the security logs” is the longest stretch of work in the chapter and had no sound under it at all.
The narration says plainly that she kept typing. Quiet, because it is under a line of banter rather than under the investigation.

Sarah going back to work after the exchange about the baby. RE-ANCHORED 2026-09-21 to '...before returning to typing', which is now where she actually resumes. The line it used to sit on reads 'Sarah temporarily paused on the keyboard' in Joshua's corrected manuscript, and keyboard clatter on the word paused would contradict the sentence carrying it.

The manuscript says a new warning tone interrupted them, so the tone must arrive before the narration, into the middle of the warmest moment in the chapter. Same asset as the earlier alert -- the same machine is calling again.

The array waking up, ONCE, from the remote initialization request. It used to sustain to the end of the chapter, and that was the same mistake chapters 2 and 3 carried: this asset is a 20-second RISE, a bed loops, so it climbed, snapped back and climbed again under the last thirty segments. A rise played once is what the moment actually is -- something enormous starting -- and the chapter ends before it would have needed to repeat.
The refusal tone before TOMBS says Request denied, so the system rejects him and then explains itself.

The second occurrence of the same clip, and the same asset again. Hearing the identical refusal twice is the information: he tried again and got exactly nowhere. This cue is why anchors carry an occurrence number.

The chapter's turn. Being locked out is not the same event as being refused, and it should not sound like it -- heavier, lower, final. After this the sound design gets out of the way and leaves the last nine segments to two voices and the rising array.
Jack entering his administrator credentials. Slightly louder than the rest: this is the keystroke the chapter turns on, and the refusal answers it.
“Jack tried his credentials again.” The same sound a second time is the information, exactly as the two denial tones are.

_removed.why: The sentence it sounded on is gone. The revised opening reads 'a second tone followed, louder than the first, and the diagnostic display flashed amber' where it used to read 'the entire console erupted with alarms'. A console erupting on an amber display is the loud version of the scene the revision removes. The two console tones and the low alert bed stay -- those are the local lab warning tones the revised text keeps.
